content: Eravacycline is indicated for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAIs). The recommended dosage is 1 mg/kg administered intravenously every 12 hours for a duration of 4 to 14 days. The intravenous infusion should be given over approximately 60 minutes. No dosage adjustment is required for patients with renal impairment. However, eravacycline is not indicated for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections. Its safety and efficacy have not been established in patients under 18 years of age. Eravacycline may reduce the effectiveness of amoxicillin and ampicillin due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Tetracyclines, including eravacycline, can interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. If used concomitantly, monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of penicillins. It is recommended to avoid or use alternative drugs in such cases. Eravacycline may also reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products, which contain bacterial spores, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibacterial agents can decrease the effectiveness of oral microbiota products if co-administered. It is advised to complete antibiotic regimens 2 to 4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Systemic retinoid use has been associated with cases of benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), some of which involved concomitant use of tetracyclines. Eravacycline levels may be decreased by magnesium sulfate, potassium chloride, or sodium sulfate due to inhibition of gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. To avoid chelation with magnesium, administer tetracyclines at least 2 hours before and no less than 6 hours after each dose. Eravacycline may increase the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely when co-administering these drugs. Zinc can decrease the levels or effects of eravacycline by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Separate the administration of oral tetracycline derivatives and oral zinc salts by at least 2 hours. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including life-threatening anaphylaxis, have been reported with eravacycline. Avoid use in patients with a history of tetracycline allergy, and discontinue treatment if an allergic reaction occurs. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinue ongoing antibacterial drug use not directed against C. difficile and initiate appropriate treatment measures. Eravacycline is structurally similar to tetracyclines and may have similar adverse reactions, including photosensitivity, pseudotumor cerebri, and anti-anabolic effects. These effects can lead to increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN), azotemia, acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, pancreatitis, and abnormal liver function tests. It may also cause overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, including fungi. Prescribing eravacycline without a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Like other tetracycline-class antibacterial drugs, eravacycline may cause discoloration of deciduous teeth and reversible inhibition of bone growth when administered during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. It is unknown if eravacycline is excreted in human breast milk. However, eravacycline and its metabolites are excreted in the milk of lactating rats. Tetracyclines are excreted in human milk, but the extent of absorption by the breastfed infant is not known. Since other antibacterial drug options are available to treat cIAI in lactating women and due to the potential for serious adverse reactions, including tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with eravacycline and for 4 days after the last dose (based on the drug's half-life).
